clinical_knowledge.topic: Prerenal Acute Kidney Injury (volume depletion) evaluation and management
core_concepts: Prompt recognition and structured assessment of Prerenal Acute Kidney Injury (volume depletion) is essential for guiding targeted diagnostic workup and clinical decision-making.
A thorough clinical history, baseline risk assessment, and targeted objective testing must be synthesized rather than relying on any single symptom in isolation.

Standard management prioritizes immediately holding nephrotoxic and renin-angiotensin-blocking agents (ACE inhibitors, NSAIDs) that impair renal autoregulation during volume depletion, followed by cautious volume repletion guided by urine output and renal function trends.
Diagnostic workup and therapeutic decisions should adhere to established clinical guidelines while accounting for patient-specific comorbidities.
diagnostic_clues: Chief Complaint: generalized weakness, decreased urination, and nausea 4 days after severe diarrhea

Key HPI features: 65F presents with severe exhaustion, nausea, and dark, sparse urine (oliguria) for the past 2 days. Had severe watery diarrhea 4 days ago after eating suspect seafood and could not keep fluids down.

Objective/Exam findings: Vitals: BP 98/62, HR 108, orthostatic drop of ~20 mmHg systolic on standing, afebrile. Dry mucous membranes, poor skin turgor. Labs: BUN 55 mg/dL, Creatinine 2.8 mg/dL (baseline 1.0), BUN:Cr ratio >20:1, FeNa <1%, urine sodium <20 mEq/L.
Current medications: Lisinopril 20mg daily, Ibuprofen 400mg TID (taken for joint pain)
common_misconceptions: Assuming that an atypical or mild presentation rules out Prerenal Acute Kidney Injury (volume depletion).
Relying solely on a single normal laboratory value or imaging result to prematurely exclude pathology.
Equating temporary symptomatic relief with full resolution of the underlying condition without completing standard evaluation.
Misattributing symptoms exclusively to Acute tubular necrosis (if prerenal injury persists untreated) without completing a comprehensive diagnostic workup.
dangerous_errors: Failing to recognize red-flag features and delaying urgent escalation or emergency intervention.
Prematurely discharging or reassuring the patient before completing appropriate diagnostic assessment.
Initiating empirical treatment without considering major patient contraindications or drug interactions.
Ignoring critical warning signs such as: Confusion or very low blood pressure — suggests more severe volume depletion.
management_principles: Check BUN, creatinine, electrolytes, and urine studies (FeNa, urine sodium) to confirm a prerenal etiology
boundaries_and_exceptions: Specific drug dosages, monitoring protocols, and referral criteria must be tailored to organ function, comorbidities, and local hospital pathways.
Atypical presentations in elderly, pediatric, or immunocompromised patients may require lower thresholds for inpatient monitoring and specialist consultation.

reference_soap.subjective:
Chief Complaint: generalized weakness, decreased urination, and nausea 4 days after severe diarrhea

65F presents with severe exhaustion, nausea, and dark, sparse urine (oliguria) for the past 2 days. Had severe watery diarrhea 4 days ago after eating suspect seafood and could not keep fluids down.
reference_soap.objective: Vitals: BP 98/62, HR 108, orthostatic drop of ~20 mmHg systolic on standing, afebrile. Dry mucous membranes, poor skin turgor. Labs: BUN 55 mg/dL, Creatinine 2.8 mg/dL (baseline 1.0), BUN:Cr ratio >20:1, FeNa <1%, urine sodium <20 mEq/L.
reference_soap.assessment: Prerenal AKI due to severe volume depletion from watery diarrhea, exacerbated by continued Lisinopril and NSAID use, which impair renal autoregulation in the setting of hypovolemia.
reference_soap.plan: Hold Lisinopril and Ibuprofen immediately. Administer cautious IV hydration. Monitor creatinine, BUN, and urine output. Refer to specialty team and provide comprehensive patient counseling.

learning_objectives: Recognize clinical features and diagnostic criteria of Prerenal Acute Kidney Injury (AKI) exacerbated by Lisinopril and NSAID use in setting of volume depletion.
Formulate prioritized differential diagnosis for generalized weakness, decreased urination, and nausea 4 days after severe diarrhea
Select appropriate laboratory and imaging studies for nephrology
Implement evidence-based acute and long-term management strategies for Prerenal Acute Kidney Injury (AKI) exacerbated by Lisinopril and NSAID use in setting of volume depletion.

teaching.one_liner: Severe fluid loss from diarrhea reduces blood flow to the kidneys, and continuing an ACE inhibitor or NSAID during this state worsens the injury — treated by holding those drugs and cautious rehydration.
differentials: Acute tubular necrosis (if prerenal injury persists untreated)
red_flags: Confusion or very low blood pressure — suggests more severe volume depletion

must_ask.say: Tell me about the diarrhea — how severe, and what do you think caused it?
Have you been able to keep fluids down?
Are you taking any blood pressure pills or pain relievers?
Do you feel weak or dizzy, especially standing up?

history.answer: Doctor, I've had terrible watery diarrhea for the past four days, and for the last two days I've barely made any urine and feel completely exhausted.
The diarrhea hit me four days ago, and over the last two days I've only urinated once or twice a day in tiny amounts, barely a few spoonfuls each time.
It started after I ate some raw seafood four days ago; I had over ten episodes of watery diarrhea a day and vomited twice, so I could barely keep water down.
Yes, my mouth feels like sandpaper and I've been desperately thirsty, but whenever I try to drink water I feel nauseated.
I get extremely lightheaded and my vision darkens every time I try to sit up or stand out of bed.
The little urine I did pass was very dark brown, like strong black tea, but I didn't see blood or foam in it.
No, there is no pain or burning when I urinate, and my lower belly does not feel full or bloated at all.
No, I don't have any pain in my back or flanks, and I've never had kidney stones before.
No, my legs and face haven't swollen at all, and I have not felt short of breath.
I've been feeling persistent nausea and lost my appetite since the diarrhea started, but no itching, hiccups, or confusion.
My heart has been beating really fast in my chest, and my arms and legs feel heavy and completely drained of energy.
No, I haven't had any fever or chills, skin rash, or bloody phlegm.
No, I haven't had a sore throat, runny nose, or any skin boils or infections recently.
No, I haven't done heavy exercise, had any falls, or remained immobilized on the floor.
No, I haven't had any CT scans, dye injections, or procedures recently.
I take Lisinopril 20 milligrams every morning for high blood pressure, and I take Ibuprofen 400 milligrams three times a day for my arthritic knees, which I continued taking even while sick.
No, I have never had heart failure, liver cirrhosis, or any kidney problems in the past.
No, I have never had any pelvic cancers, pelvic surgery, or radiation therapy.
I have had high blood pressure for ten years and osteoarthritis in both knees for five years.
I had an appendectomy when I was twenty-five, but no other surgeries or hospitalizations.
I have no known allergies to medications, foods, or materials.
I have never smoked cigarettes in my life.
I might have a glass of wine on holidays, but I haven't had any alcohol in months.
I am a retired teacher and live with my husband in a quiet apartment.
My father had high blood pressure and passed away from a stroke in his eighties, but no one in my family had kidney disease.
I went through menopause around age fifty-two and haven't had any vaginal bleeding since.
I thought this might just be a lingering stomach flu with severe dehydration from the bad seafood.
I'm really frightened that my kidneys have shut down and suffered permanent damage because I stopped peeing.
I was hoping you could give me IV fluids to rehydrate me and flush out my kidneys so they start working again.

exam.finding: Lethargic, ill-appearing elderly female lying in bed with dry lips and sunken eyes.
Blood pressure 98/62 mmHg, heart rate 108 beats/min, respiratory rate 18 breaths/min, body temperature 36.7°C, SpO2 98% on room air.
Supine blood pressure 98/62 mmHg with pulse 108 beats/min drops to 78/50 mmHg with pulse 126 beats/min upon standing, accompanied by lightheadedness.
Pale, very dry oral mucosa with cracked lips and a dry, furrowed tongue; pharynx is clear.
Flat neck veins with jugular venous pressure below 5 cm H2O, not visible even at 30 degrees.
Tachycardic regular rhythm without murmurs, rubs, or gallops.
Clear breath sounds bilaterally without crackles, wheezes, or rhonchi.
Soft, non-distended, mildly tender diffusely without guarding or rebound tenderness; no suprapubic distension or palpable bladder.
Tympanic throughout with dullness absent above the symphysis pubis; no shifting dullness.
No peripheral edema in bilateral lower extremities.
Significantly decreased skin turgor with delayed skin recoil lasting over 3 seconds on the clavicle and forearm; no rash.
Bilateral Heberden and Bouchard nodes on distal and proximal interphalangeal joints without acute erythema, warmth, or active effusion.
Alert and oriented to person, place, and time, though responding with mild psychomotor slowing due to fatigue.
